rows.searchedFor: if I want the whole company to start using some new app, how do I get that approved?
rows.answer:
The handbook's process for proposing a new company-wide tool starts with a low-risk trial and a proposal in Company Internal.

- First, try the tool in a low-risk context: somewhere it is easily replaced and doesn't involve sensitive data. If you're unsure what information can be shared at this stage, check with #legal first.[1]
- The trial is meant to check that the tool works as well as you expect, to help you understand the consequences of introducing it, to learn what data it may have access to, and to give others a way to see it in action.[2]
- Second, open a pull request in Company Internal and, at the same time, open an issue describing why we should adopt the tool. Anyone proposing a new vendor should think about the impact on the whole company, not just their team or use case.[3]

Once a decision is made to adopt the tool, the person proposing it is responsible for coordinating the next steps.[4] Those steps include:
- Negotiating business terms with the vendor, such as cost, number of licenses or usage terms and limits, contract length, and implementation or onboarding details.[5]
- Sending the vendor's documents through legal review before anything is signed, once the business terms are mostly settled.[6]
- Posting in #legal as soon as it looks like we'll move forward, to say a decision has been made, business terms are being negotiated, and contract documents will be shared shortly.[7]

If the vendor is a subprocessor, customers must receive 14 days' notice after the agreement is finalized before the vendor can be used in production.[8] If you're unsure whether a tool qualifies as a subprocessor, check with #legal early.[9]

This process doesn't cover cheap decisions. A cheap decision is one that can be easily completed or reversed, or one that only affects your work and not other people's, and those follow the software section of the spending money page.[10]

rows.searchedFor: if my PR touches a github actions workflow, does it need a special reviewer?
rows.answer:
Great care should be taken when writing or modifying a GitHub Actions workflow, because Actions can access (and exfiltrate) secrets scoped to the repo, and workflows are scanned with Semgrep and CodeQL for common misconfigurations.[1]

What the handbook does say about review in general:
- Almost all PRs made to PostHog repositories need a review from another engineer.[2]
- You can request a review from someone relevant.[3]
- If the workflow change is for a GitHub App, you can send a message in #team-security if you need help setting up a new GitHub App.[4]

rows.searchedFor: is there a rubric or list of criteria I need to hit to move up here?
rows.answer:
The question is ambiguous ("here"), but the handbook's Salesforce opportunity stages do have exit criteria for advancing, so I'll answer on that basis.

Bolded exit criteria are the minimum standard for an opportunity to advance stages (for typically smaller, more transactional deals).[1] Exit criteria by stage:

- Problem Agreement: identified and implicated pain with specific, quantifiable metrics (time/money/risk); a documented, real-consequence answer to "What happens if you do nothing?"; and the buyer explicitly saying "This is a problem we need to solve" (not just "interesting").[2]
- Solution Agreement: active product usage or a completed POC/trial; a clear, documentable decision for PostHog (with or without comparing alternatives); the Economic Buyer identified (name + title); and a Champion identified (name).[3]
- Priority Agreement: budget confirmed (amount range or "yes, funded"); decision process mapped (who approves, what steps, timeline); the Economic Buyer saying this is a priority (exact quote documented); champion tested (evidence they're advocating internally); and a compelling event known (budget cycle, launch, renewal, etc.).[4]
- Commercial Agreement: price agreed in writing (email/quote with amount + terms); all commercial terms agreed (payment terms, contract length, prepaid amount); and the paper process mapped (legal, security, procurement steps + owners + timeline).[5]
- Vendor Approval: contract signed.[6]

These stages apply to the New and Existing Business Record Types, and stages differ by Opportunity Record Type.[7] More detail on the stages and exit criteria is in a spreadsheet the handbook links.[1]

rows.searchedFor: a customer runs posthog inside their browser extension and their bill is way higher than it should be, how do they fix it?
rows.answer:
The handbook's Wildfire Systems case study says extensions handle session and identity persistence in a way that caused unusually high event volume and feature flag calls, which inflated billing[1]. The recommended fixes for extension developers are:

- Persist the ID manually by using chrome.storage.local to store a UUID.[2] Wildfire's UUID was generated once, then reused across all extension contexts.[3]
- Bootstrap identity by passing the UUID during posthog.init() with bootstrap.distinctID.[4]
- Only call identify() if the ID has changed.[5] Wildfire checked if the existing distinct_id matched the UUID before calling identify().[6]
- Reduce /flags usage by using bootstrap.featureFlags and disabling polling if needed.[7]
- Monitor proactively using the "My PostHog Billable Usage" dashboard.[8] At Wildfire it showed real-time data to verify that fixes worked.[9]

The cause is that each new runtime context re-initialized PostHog without access to prior storage[10]. That created a new anonymous ID on each wake cycle[11], and identify() was then called each time[12], which refreshed feature flags[13].

The handbook also notes that raising the billing limit mid-cycle did not retroactively unlock flags; only new requests after the monthly reset were allowed.[14]

rows.searchedFor: how do tickets get divvied up on the support team? does everyone work every product?
rows.answer:
No, not strictly. Everyone shares some work, but SMEs also own specific product groups.

- All technical support engineers, regardless of SME ownership, work on Analytics products, which are shared because they make up the highest proportion of tickets.[1] They also work on unclassified tickets, which should be updated with the correct product group where possible.[2]
- Beyond that, SMEs own specific product groups, with one person from EU and one from NA per group to maintain timezone coverage.[3]
- The product groups listed are Flags, Data, Replay, Observability + AI & client libraries, and Analytics.[4][5][6][7][8]

Day to day, SMEs start with their SME views, then move to the Technical support shared view, which has all tickets the technical support team is responsible for.[9] They aren't locked into only their SME products: if caught up, they can help with the shared queue, and if swamped, they can ask for help with their SME queue.[10]

When picking tickets, avoid cherry-picking and take the ticket closest to breaching response targets.[11] Support team members working across multiple queues often assign tickets to themselves, and assign them back to the team/group when escalating.[12]

For new hires, they usually spend the first few weeks focused only on product and web analytics tickets, until they're more familiar with the platform.[13]

rows.searchedFor: what's the cutoff for a new lead to get worked by sales instead of just going self-serve?
rows.answer:
The handbook's sales-assist threshold is $20K ARR: if a lead will be too small (<$20k) to go through the sales-led process and you can't get that information from them, you should route them to self-serve.[1] The qualification checklist uses the same figure, asking how large the company is, what its revenue is, and whether it has raised funding (i.e. will they pay >$20k for PostHog?)[2]

Some other factors also affect whether a lead stays hands-on:
- If their usage volume is around 5 million monthly events and 100,000 recordings, they should be hands-on.[3]
- If they want an annual commitment, keep them in the hands-on pipeline.[4]
- If they need help with a guided evaluation and their potential value is high enough, create a Slack Connect channel and keep them in the hands-on pipeline.[4]
- If none of these apply, move them to self-serve.[5]

For product-led leads (existing customers), if you think they have potential to end up paying more than $20k a year, you should reach out to introduce yourself and offer help.[6]

rows.answer:
Yes: before reaching out, search for the company in Vitally, and if they already have an assigned Account Executive or CSM, give that person a heads-up, since they might already be working on something with the customer or have extra context on what to ask about.[1] If no one is assigned in Vitally, you're clear to reach out directly.[2]

- Some customers have a dedicated Slack channel, which is usually the fastest way to coordinate; otherwise, send an email.[3]

rows.searchedFor: Do we give customers anything in exchange for participating in an interview for a story on the website?
rows.answer:
The handbook says once the case study is merged and live on the website, the last step is to send a merch credit to the participants as a thank you.[1] It also says PostHog typically thanks customers who participate in case studies and collab content by sending them a merch voucher.[2]

This is a thank-you after publication, not a trade for participating. The handbook says PostHog doesn't offer additional discounts in exchange for a case study, as paying for case studies can devalue them.[3]

rows.searchedFor: how did we score on the last staff survey compared to the benchmark?
rows.answer:
- The benchmark is Culture Amp's 'new tech' companies with fewer than 200 people, and PostHog takes the average score out of 5 and multiplies it by 20 to get a percentage that can be compared with it.[1]
- A summary of the results is reported in an Issue using a template, and the handbook says you can view the latest survey results there.[2]
- Only the People & Ops and Exec teams have access to the full list of responses.[3]
